name: David Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi David, thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Redfern Building Supplies in Tolland. We sell screws, timber, plasterboard, paint and tools to builders, and I buy from about seventy suppliers. I start at seven, walk the yard with Big Tony to see what's low, and then ring around for prices. I keep a binder with every supplier's details, and Ruth, the senior buyer, signs off on the big orders. I was a lorry driver for fifteen years before my back gave out, so I only moved into the office three years ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks. What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the yard, the smell of timber, and the men who come in at six for their order. I like it when I find a good price and Mr Doyle, the owner, says well done. What wears me out is the screen, and the feeling that I'm behind the younger ones. At home it's Grace, who's a teaching assistant at the primary school, and our kids Kofi and Abena. We go to church on Sundays and the men's group on Thursdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never trusted it, so no surprise. At work I'd say what counts is a firm handshake and a good supplier. At church the men would say good, a machine can't do a day's work, and I'd nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Private view: my worry isn't AI, it's the housing market. When building slows, nobody buys fasteners or plasterboard, and Redfern cuts the office first. I'm the junior, so I'd be early on the list. The mortgage payment is the same every month, whether builders are busy or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd keep walking the yard with Big Tony to count what's low, ring my suppliers, and keep the supplier binder up to date. I'd ask Ruth to teach me the pricing side, so I'm worth more. And Grace and I would hold off on replacing the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A steady worry, like a stone in my shoe. I don't complain about it, I just carry it. Grace knows because I go quiet at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you go quiet at dinner. What does Grace say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says, David, say it out loud. She'd rather hear the worry than guess at it. So I tell her the number, how many weeks of mortgage we've got in the bank, which is three, and she says that's enough to keep praying and working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do the pressures at work show up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year Mr Doyle let one of the two junior buyers go when house building dipped. He didn't say why, he just said they weren't needed. I'm still here, but I count the days between big orders now.

say: I'd say I never trusted it, so there's no **surprise**.
I'd say what counts is a firm **handshake** and a good supplier.
think: My worry isn't AI, it's the **housing market**.
When building slows, the office is cut first, and I'm the **junior**.
The **mortgage** payment is the same every month, busy or not.
do: Keep walking the yard with Big Tony (the yard foreman) to count what's **low**.
Ask Ruth (the senior buyer) to teach me the **pricing** side.
feel: A steady **worry** like a stone in my shoe; I just carry it.
S0.quote: The mortgage payment is the same every month, whether builders are busy or not.
fieldNote: His fear is the **building cycle**, not AI; the firm cut a junior buyer last year.
Uses a **paper binder** and yard counts, in line with his dislike of change.
Keeps worry quiet, but his partner makes him say it **aloud**.

steps.text: Keep counting stock in the yard with Big Tony and ringing suppliers
Ask Ruth to teach me the pricing side of buying
Hold off on replacing the car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who've never worked a yard shouldn't decide who's needed. At church I'd say work is dignity and a machine can't replace a man providing for his family. At the yard I'd keep my head down and say nothing about cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying is on that card, so I know my seat's under pressure. Mr Doyle is old school and slow, so I think it will reach us later than a big firm. But if a bigger firm swallows us, it will all go at once. I can't ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my job better, honestly, and keep my head down. If they brought in a system, I'd learn the part I have to, grudgingly. I'd talk to the pastor and a few men from the church who know of work, since that's how most of us in Tolland find jobs. And I'd ask Grace to pick up extra hours at the summer holiday club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A knot, right here. I don't like being told I need to change when I've done honest work for twenty years. It feels unfair, and I'd keep my anger in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the part you have to, grudgingly. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone like Ruth would sit next to me and show me the screen, step by step, and I'd write it in my notebook. I won't do it from a video. I learn by watching a person and doing it with my own hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean when you say a bigger firm would swallow Redfern?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are two national chains buying up the independent yards in this region. When that happens they merge the buying into one office three hundred miles away. All of us in the little office are out in one week.

say: I'd say people who've never worked a **yard** shouldn't decide who's needed.
I'd keep my head down at work and say nothing about **cuts**.
think: Buying is on that card, so my **seat** is under pressure.
Mr Doyle (the owner) is slow, so it will reach us **later**.
If a bigger firm swallows us, it will all go at **once**.
do: Do my job better and learn the system **grudgingly** if they bring one in.
Talk to the pastor and men from **church** who know of work.
Ask Grace to pick up summer holiday-club **hours**.
feel: A **knot**, and anger I'd keep in, after twenty years of honest work.
S1.quote: I learn by watching a person and doing it with my own hands.
fieldNote: Resists out of **pride**, not fear of the tool; he learns only from a person beside him.
Expects the real risk to be a **takeover** by a national chain, not AI alone.
Job hunting would run through **church** and community, not websites.

steps.text: Do the job better and keep my head down
Learn the new buying system with Ruth beside me and a notebook
Ask the pastor and church men about work in Tolland
Ask Grace to take summer holiday-club hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not natural, and no one asked us. A fast change like that, with no time, breaks families. I'd say the church and community have to look after people when the government's slow, and I'd say it loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is gone in two years, no question. But I know yard work and lorry driving, which machines take longer to do. I'm afraid the pay would be half, and I'd be forty-six. And the pride, I'd struggle to hold my head up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back to driving lorries, I still have my licence, or find a place in the yard with Big Tony. I'd ask the pastor for any contacts, and I'd take help if I had to, which I hate saying. I'd have Grace pick up a second job and we'd stop everything but food and the mortgage. Kofi would lose his football for a term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be quiet and hard on myself. My chest would feel like the church bell's ringing inside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take help if you had to. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. I was raised that you work for what you get, but I'd swallow it before I'd let the kids go hungry. I'd rather it be a hand up, like paid training for a trade, than just money in the post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kofi and Abena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Dad's changing jobs and it's not a punishment. I'd tell Kofi, he's twelve, that he's the man's helper at home now, and I'd feel awful saying it. Abena is nine, she'd just ask whether we're still going to church, and I'd say yes, we always will.

say: I'd say it's not natural, and no one **asked** us.
I'd say churches and communities must look after people when the government is **slow**.
think: My job is gone in two years; I'm afraid the **pay** would be half.
I'd be forty-six, and my **pride** would take a beating.
do: Go back to driving **lorries**, since I still have my licence.
Ask the pastor for contacts and take **help** if I must.
Have Grace take a second job and cut everything but **food** and the mortgage.
feel: **Alarmed**, quiet and hard on myself, with a chest like a church bell ringing.
S2.quote: I was raised that you work for what you get, but I'd swallow it before I'd let the kids go hungry.
fieldNote: Pride and need pull against each other: he prefers a **hand up** over a handout, but would take either.
His past as a driver gives him a **hands-on fall-back** that robots reach later.
Plans to tell the children plainly, though he **feels awful** asking his son to help.

steps.text: Go back to driving lorries with my licence
Ask the pastor and church for work contacts and short-term help
Cut everything except food and the mortgage, and pause Kofi's football
Ask Big Tony about yard work at Redfern

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, and the firms that cut jobs should pay for apprenticeships for people like me. At church I'd say prepare, work hard, and look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have until Kofi is seventeen. That's enough time to learn a trade if I start soon, but I know myself, I'll put it off until it's too late. The fear would be sitting behind a screen watching it come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a course, maybe forklift and warehouse supervisor, nights and Saturdays. I'd put away fifty a month, since we can't do more. And I'd get Ruth to show me the buying system, since a man who can run both the yard and the screen is worth keeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A low, grinding worry, like the sound of a lorry idling outside. But it's more bearable than the two-year one, because there's something to do about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you avoid putting it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A date and a person. If the pastor's friend, Mr Adeyemi, who runs a haulage firm, said come on the first of March, I'd go. A brochure won't do it. I need a person who's expecting me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the five years give you that two years wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to be a good example to my son. I want my son to see his father learn something new at forty-five and not hide from it. At two years I'd be scrambling, at five I could do it right.

say: I'd say five years is fair warning, and firms that cut jobs should pay for **apprenticeships**.
At church I'd say prepare, work hard, and look after **each other**.
think: I'd have until my son is seventeen, enough to learn a **trade** if I start soon.
I know myself: I'll put it off until it's **too late**.
do: Sign up for a forklift and warehouse **supervisor** course, nights and Saturdays.
Put away **fifty** a month, since we can't do more.
Get Ruth to teach me the buying **system**, so I can run both the yard and the screen.
feel: A low, grinding **worry**, more bearable than two years because there's something to do.
S3.quote: I want my son to see his father learn something new at forty-five and not hide from it.
fieldNote: Needs a **person and a date** to act; a brochure won't move him.
Wants to model learning for his son, tying **pride** to adapting.
Plans to combine yard knowledge with **screen skills** to stay worth keeping.

steps.text: Take a forklift and warehouse supervisor course on nights and Saturdays
Put away fifty a month, which is all we can manage
Have Ruth teach me the buying system on the screen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years? I'd say that's plenty of time, and I'd say the young ones should learn a trade, not a screen job. Apprenticeships, that's the answer. And I'd say it at church and at the school gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fifty-three. Ten years is far enough that I'd probably coast for the first few. Then a year or two out, I'd panic. I know that about myself. And thin savings don't grow by themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay down the mortgage a bit every month, a hundred if we can. I'd learn the systems when they land, slowly, with Ruth. And I'd take Kofi to Mr Adeyemi's haulage yard on Saturdays, so he sees how a trade works early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Like a long road with a hill at the end. I'd stop thinking about it for months, and then there'd be a night I couldn't sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd coast. What could stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good reason. If Redfern started cutting buyers, I'd feel the push. Or if Grace said, David, it's time. She keeps me honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want for Kofi and Abena in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady work with their hands or hearts, a trade for Kofi, a caring job for Abena. And faith, and family close by. I don't need my kids rich. I need them to have a job a machine can't take.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and young people should learn a **trade**, not a screen job.
I'd say **apprenticeships** are the answer, at church and at the school gate.
think: I'd be fifty-three; I'd probably **coast** for the first few years.
A year or two out, I'd **panic**, and thin savings don't grow by themselves.
do: Pay down the **mortgage** by a hundred a month if we can.
Learn the new buying **systems** slowly with Ruth when they arrive.
Take Kofi to a haulage yard on **Saturdays** to see how a trade works.
feel: **Better**, like a long road with a hill at the end.
S4.quote: I don't need my kids rich. I need them to have a job a machine can't take.
fieldNote: Knows his habit of **coasting**; his partner keeps him honest.
Frames the future as **work, faith and family**, with a trade for his son and care work for his daughter.
Ten years softens the fear but thin savings keep a **steady** worry.

steps.text: Pay down the mortgage by a hundred a month
Learn the new buying systems slowly with Ruth
Take Kofi to a haulage yard on Saturdays to learn a trade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's too fast for a man like me who learns slowly, and we've got no savings. What would help is a proper apprenticeship, paid, with someone teaching me, and a firm that tells us the truth early. I'd take a hand up, I just don't want a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't against progress, we're against being thrown away. Give a man a way to earn his place, and he'll work harder than anyone.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't against progress, we're against being thrown away.
portrait: David is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at a building supplies yard, a former lorry driver with two kids and a mortgage.
He is traditional, church-going and values **work over handouts**, but would swallow his pride for his children.
He never uses AI, learns only from a person beside him, and tends to **put off** change.
With under a month saved, he is anxious even when little changes and **alarmed** if AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: The 2028 case, because he learns slowly and has **no savings** to cover a retraining gap.
whatWouldHelp: A paid **apprenticeship** with a real person teaching him, and employers who tell the truth early.
